Model reference

Source: vignettes/models.Rmd
models.Rmd

This vignette states, for every model of mortensor, the model equation, the estimation method, how the forecast is generated, the defaults, and which sources of uncertainty the forecast draws contain. It is meant as the basis of a methods section. summary() of a fitted model prints the same information for the actual fit, mt_parameters() returns the estimates.

library(mortensor)
x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019)
summary(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x))
#> Lee-Carter
#>   data: 2 strata; ages 30 to 100+; periods 1995-2019
#>   model and uncertainty:
#>     log m(x,t) = a(x) + b(x) k(t), estimated by Poisson maximum likelihood
#>     (Brouhns et al. 2002; Lee and Carter 1992). k(t) follows a random walk with
#>     drift; draws include its innovations and the uncertainty of the drift. a(x)
#>     and b(x) are fixed (parameter uncertainty with bootstrapped()). Jump-off:
#>     fitted rates.
#>   fit: Poisson deviance 3371.3 on 3550 cells (0.95 per cell); 3.9% of deviance residuals beyond +/-2

Notation: m(x,t,i) is the central death rate at age x in year t in stratum i (deaths divided by exposure), D deaths, E exposures.

Data steps that affect every model

Step What mortensor does Function
Exposures mid-year population, or the mean of two 1 January or 31 December populations mt_as_exposure(type = )
Suppressed cells raking (iterative proportional fitting; Deming and Stephan 1940) of the missing counts to published totals, within optional bounds mt_fill_suppressed()
Unknown ages distributed over the age groups of the same stratum and year in proportion to the known deaths mt_data()
Ungrouping penalised composite link model with exposures (Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015) or spline methods mt_ungroup(), step_ungroup()
Smoothing over age (Poisson P-splines, Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004; Whittaker; GAM), over time (Whittaker) or the age-period surface (P-splines; quasi-Poisson te(age, year) GAM, Wood 2017); age 0 is not smoothed; models are fitted to the smoothed rates, their observation noise, residuals and backtest scales come from the raw rates mt_smooth(), step_smooth(), mt_smooth_check()
Zero deaths models on log rates use 0.5 deaths in a cell without deaths

All preprocessing steps given as prep are refitted on every training window of a backtest.

Single-population models

Lee-Carter: lee_carter()

log m(x,t) = a(x) + b(x) k(t), with sum b(x) = 1 and sum k(t) = 0 (Lee and Carter 1992).

  • Estimation: Poisson maximum likelihood (default; Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002) or SVD of the log rates (method = "svd", as demography::lca()), with k(t) re-estimated to match the observed total deaths (adjust = "dt"), the deaths by age ("dxt", Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002) or life expectancy ("e0", Lee and Miller 2001). choose_period = TRUE fits the model to the longest recent period over which k(t) was close to linear (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002). Age groups without any death get a constant rate of 0.5 deaths over the training period and b(x) = 0; when the Poisson likelihood has no finite maximum (very sparse counts), b(x) is shrunk towards equal shares by a ridge penalty. Both are reported as warnings.
  • Forecast: k(t) follows a random walk with drift; the drift and the innovation variance are estimated from the year-to-year changes of k(t).
  • Jump-off: fitted rates of the last year (default) or observed rates (jump_off = "observed").
  • Uncertainty in the draws: innovations of k(t) and the uncertainty of its drift. a(x) and b(x) are fixed; bootstrap = TRUE or bootstrapped() adds their uncertainty.

Random walk with drift: rwd()

Each age: log m(x,t) = log m(x,t-1) + mu(x) + e(x,t).

  • Estimation: drift as the mean year-to-year change (over the last drift_window years); innovations are resampled vectors of observed changes across ages (innovations = "bootstrap", keeps the correlation between ages) or normal ("gaussian").
  • Uncertainty: innovations and drift. The observed changes contain the Poisson noise of two years, so the intervals are wide where deaths are few, and over long horizons very wide.
  • observation_noise = TRUE: log rate = level + noise, the level a random walk with drift (local level model). The noise variance is the Poisson part (one over the deaths) plus an extra part common to all ages; the level variance is estimated from the variance and first autocovariance of the changes and partly pooled across ages (ages with few deaths borrow from the median of the others). The level is Kalman filtered; draws include level, drift and, for predictive draws, noise.

Functional demographic model: hyndman_ullah()

Calls demography::fdm() (Hyndman and Ullah 2007): smoothed log rates decomposed into a mean function and functional principal components, whose scores are forecast with time-series models. Draws are simulated from the fitted model. Its intervals are those of the simulated paths, which are somewhat narrower at short horizons than demography’s analytic intervals (see the comparison vignette).

Time series per age: arima_series(), ets_series()

Benchmarks that model the observed log rate of every age as a separate time series with the forecast package (Hyndman and Khandakar 2008): an ARIMA model chosen by forecast::auto.arima() (drift allowed) or an exponential smoothing model chosen by forecast::ets() (damped trends allowed). Uncertainty: simulated future paths of the fitted models, so the intervals grow with the horizon; ages are simulated independently and parameter uncertainty is not included. The series are observed rates, so their draws already contain observation noise.

StMoMo models: stmomo()

Calls StMoMo::fit() and simulate() (Villegas, Kaishev and Millossovich 2018) for the Lee-Carter, CBD, APC, RH and M6 families. Draws contain the period and cohort index uncertainty that StMoMo simulates; parameter uncertainty is not included.

Bayesian age-period-cohort model: apc_bayes()

Calls bamp::bamp() (Schmid and Held 2007): logit death probability = age + period + cohort effects with random-walk priors of order 1 or 2, binomial likelihood, MCMC. Convergence is checked with the Gelman-Rubin statistic of the identified quantities (reported by mt_parameters() as rhat); chains that have not converged are refitted with longer runs. Uncertainty: posterior samples of the forecast rates, including the uncertainty of the parameters and of the random walks of period and cohort effects; predictive draws add Poisson and extra-Poisson noise as for the other models of smooth rates. Each stratum is fitted separately. apc_select() compares random-walk orders by DIC.

Models for several populations

Li-Lee: li_lee()

log m(x,t,i) = a(x,i) + B(x) K(t) + b(x,i) k(t,i) (Li and Lee 2005).

  • Estimation: the common factor B(x) K(t) is a Lee-Carter model (SVD, k refitted to deaths) of the pooled deaths and exposures of the strata in a group (common_by, for example one common factor per sex); the stratum factors come from an SVD of the residual log rates.
  • Forecast: K(t) random walk with drift; each k(t,i) an AR(1) process without intercept, |phi| <= 0.99, so the deviations of a stratum from the common trend stay bounded (“coherent” in the sense that the strata do not diverge).
  • Uncertainty: innovations and drift of K(t), innovations of the AR(1) processes (independent across strata). a, b, B and phi are fixed.

Product-ratio: product_ratio()

The same structure on the geometric mean of the strata (common factor) and their ratios to it (Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013), with Lee-Carter components in place of functional data models.

Tucker3 and cause shares (experimental)

tucker3() decomposes the array of log rates [age, period, stratum] (or of the log-ratio coordinates of life-table deaths, transform = "coda") into factor matrices and a core; the period factors are forecast as a multivariate random walk with drift or with ARIMA/ETS models, and the in-sample residual variation is added to the draws. cause_shares() forecasts all-cause mortality with any model and the shares of causes with a Tucker model of their isometric log-ratio coordinates, so the causes add up to all causes in every draw. Neither has a published evaluation for mortality; compare them with the models above in a backtest.

Jump-off: anchored()

Forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year for most models. anchored() moves the start towards the observed level of the last years years for any model: the log ratio of observed to fitted deaths per age and stratum, shrunk towards the stratum mean where deaths are few, multiplies the draws with a weight that fades out over decay years. mt_jump_off() reports the step between the last observed (and fitted) year and the first forecast year.

Combining models

Ensembles: ensemble()

A mixture of the predictive distributions of its components: each draw comes from one component, for all strata at once, chosen with probabilities equal to the weights (equal, inverse CRPS of an inner backtest, or stacking). The mixture contains the uncertainty of each component and the disagreement between them.

Reconciled forecasts: reconciled()

Forecasts of all nodes of a hierarchy (bottom strata and their totals) are made to add up draw by draw: bottom-up sums, or projections of the base forecasts with weights from their variances (WLS), the shrunk covariance (MinT; Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos and Hyndman 2019), the structure (Hyndman et al. 2011) or equal weights (OLS). Deaths add up over every hierarchy variable; exposures add up over variables that divide the population and are shared by the levels of variables such as causes of death (additive = "rates"). The exposures of the forecast years are those of the last observed year unless projections are given.

Calibration on recent years: calibrated()

Refits a model at several origins in the last years (default 10) of the training data, compares its forecasts with the observed rates of that window, and rescales the spread of the draws around their median per cell by a factor s(h) = s1 h^gamma that minimises the CRPS (or the interval score of one interval), with the Poisson and extra-Poisson variation of the observations as in a backtest (minimum-CRPS estimation; Gneiting et al. 2005). Optionally a drift correction is estimated as well. Ranks within each cell are kept, so the draws remain paths. Calibration widens models that were persistently too narrow (Lee-Carter on England & Wales: 95% coverage 0.75 to 0.88 in backtests) and can narrow mixtures that were already wide.

Bootstrap and tuning: bootstrapped(), tuned()

bootstrapped() refits a model to Poisson resamples of the deaths (parameter uncertainty, including preprocessing with type = "data"). tuned() chooses settings (for example the rank) by an inner rolling-origin backtest on the training data only. The fitting period matters for Lee-Carter forecasts when the pace of decline changed (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002); step_window(years) makes it a preprocessing step that a backtest compares across windows.

Sources of uncertainty at a glance

Model Index innovations Drift Parameters Poisson noise Extra noise
lee_carter() yes yes with bootstrap = TRUE predictive draws predictive draws
rwd() yes (observed changes) yes no contained in the changes contained in the changes
rwd(observation_noise = TRUE) yes (level) yes no predictive draws predictive draws
arima_series(), ets_series() yes as the fitted model no contained in the series contained in the series
li_lee(), product_ratio() yes (common and stratum) common factor no predictive draws predictive draws
tucker3() yes (period factors) yes no predictive draws residual variation and predictive draws
cause_shares() of the total model and the share factors yes no predictive draws residual variation and predictive draws
hyndman_ullah() yes as fdm no predictive draws predictive draws
stmomo() yes yes no predictive draws predictive draws
apc_bayes() yes posterior yes (posterior) predictive draws predictive draws
ensemble() of the components of the components of the components, plus model choice of the components of the components
bootstrapped() of the base model of the base model yes as the base model as the base model
reconciled() of the base model, projected bottom strata, summed bottom strata, summed
calibrated() of the base model, rescaled rescaled (optional correction) as the base model as the base model
anchored() of the base model of the base model as the base model as the base model

Predictive draws (predictive = TRUE, always used in backtests) describe observable rates. For models of smooth rates they add Poisson deaths given the exposures and an extra-Poisson part estimated from the in-sample residual variance. For models of observed rates (rwd() without observation_noise, arima_series(), ets_series()) the draws already describe observable rates and nothing is added. Forecast draws of models of smooth rates without predictive describe the underlying rates.

Evaluation

mt_backtest() refits preprocessing and model at each origin and scores predictive draws against the observed log rates of the test years with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; Gneiting and Raftery 2007), the weighted interval score (Bracher et al. 2021), interval coverage, the probability integral transform and the absolute error of the median. Cells with estimated (suppressed) deaths are not scored unless score_estimated = TRUE.
